'''Karl Wieghardt''' (born 25 July 1942, in [[Göttingen]]) is a [[Germans|German]] [[inorganic chemist]] and emeritus director of the [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Energy Conversion]] in [[Mülheim an der Ruhr|Mülheim]].  He was active in the preparation and detailed characterization of models for iron and manganese [[metalloenzyme]]s, metal complexes of [[noninnocent ligand]]s, and magnetic interactions in polynuclear metal complexes.

== Early life and education==
Wieghardt was born in 1942 in [[Göttingen]], Germany, the son of the physicist [[:de:Karl Wieghardt (Physiker)|Karl Wieghardt]] and grandson of the mathematician also named [[:de:Karl Wieghardt (Mathematiker)|Karl Wieghardt]].<ref name=":0" /> From 1947-1952, Wieghardt lived in England as his father was working at the [[Admiralty Research Laboratory|Admiralty Research Laboratory of the British Navy]] in [[Teddington]].<ref name=":0" /> While in the UK, he attended elementary school in [[Elstead]], [[Surrey]].<ref name=":0" /> Following the nuclear espionage affair surrounding [[Klaus Fuchs]], Wieghardt's father was dismissed from the Admiralty Research Laboratory, and he moved his family back to Germany.<ref name=":0" /> At the age of 12, Wieghardt obtained a chemistry kit as a Christmas present from his parents, then proceeded to set his basement on fire. His parents then forbade him from doing or studying chemistry for the next eight years.<ref name=":1">{{Citation|title=Voices of Inorganic Chemistry - Karl Weighardt|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bqBQmMuooZI|language=en|access-date=2021-05-17}}</ref> In 1962, Wieghardt graduated from the [[Gelehrtenschule des Johanneums|Johanneum]] secondary school in Hamburg.

== Independent career ==
[[File:JULMUY.png|thumb|Structure of OTi(NCS)<sub>2</sub>([[1,4,7-Trimethyl-1,4,7-triazacyclononane|Me<sub>3</sub>tacn]]), first example of a titanyl complex as described by the Wieghardt group.<ref>{{cite journal|title={Mono- and Dinuclear Titanium(III)/Titanium(IV) Complexes with 1,4,7-Trimethyl-1,4,7-triazacyclononane (L). Crystal Structures of a Compositionally Disordered Green and a Blue Form of [LTiCl<sub>3</sub>]. Structures of [LTi(O)(NCS)<sub>2</sub>], [LTi(OCH<sub>3</sub>)Br<sub>2</sub>](ClO<sub>4</sub>), and [L<sub>2</sub>Ti<sub>2</sub>(O)<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>(mu-F)](PF<sub>6</sub>)|author=Axel Bodner |author2=Peter Jeske |author3=Thomas Weyhermueller |author4=Karl Wieghardt |author5=Erich Dubler |author6=Helmut Schmalle |author7=Bernhard Nuber |journal=Inorganic Chemistry|year=1992|volume=31|issue=18|pages=3737–3748|doi=10.1021/ic00044a015}}</ref>]]
Wieghardt returned to Germany, and completed his [[habilitation]] at the [[University of Heidelberg]] in 1975 with a thesis on the structural chemistry and mechanistic investigations on polynuclear cobalt-amine complexes.<ref name=":0" /> At the end of 1975, he was hired as an associate professor at the [[University of Hanover|Technical University of Hannover]].<ref name=":0" /> His work there focused on the synthesis, reactions and reaction mechanisms of vanadium and molybdenum complexes with [[hydroxylamine]] and hydroxylamine derivatives as ligands.<ref name=":0" /> In 1981 he moved to the [[Ruhr University Bochum]] as professor. It was at this stage of his career that he expanded the size of his research group, and moved into the field of bioinorganic chemistry, synthesizing transition metal complexes that act as analogs for [[metalloprotein]] active sites.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wieghardt|first1=Karl|last2=Pohl|first2=Klaus|last3=Gebert|first3=Walter|date=1983|title=[(C6H15N3)Fe2(μ-O)(μ-CH3CO2)2]2+ a Dinuclear Iron, (III)Complex with a Metazidohemerythrin-Type Structure|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/anie.198307271|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition in English|language=en|volume=22|issue=9|page=727|doi=10.1002/anie.198307271|issn=1521-3773|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chaudhury|first1=Phalguni|last2=Wieghardt|first2=Karl|last3=Nuber|first3=Bernhard|last4=Weiss|first4=Johannes|date=1985|title=[L2Fe(μ-OH)(μ-CH3CO2)2](ClO4)·H2O, a Model Compound for the Diiron Centers in Deoxyhemerythrin|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/anie.198507781|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition in English|volume=24|issue=9|pages=778–779|doi=10.1002/anie.198507781|issn=1521-3773|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Wieghardt went on to popularize the utility of [[triazacyclononane|1,4,7-triazacyclononane]] and its derivatives as ligands for biomimetic transition metal complexes.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Chaudhuri|first1=P.|last2=Wieghardt|first2=K.|year=1987|editor-last=Lippard|editor-first=Stephen J.|chapter=The Chemistry of 1,4,7-Triazacyclononane and Related Tridentate Macrocyclic Compounds|title=Progress in Inorganic Chemistry|location=Hoboken, NJ, USA|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Inc.|volume=35|pages=329–436|doi=10.1002/9780470166369.ch4|isbn=978-0-470-16636-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=1,4,7-Triazacyclononane and N,N',N"-Trimethyl-1,4,7-triazacyclononane - Two Versatile Macrocycles for the Synthesis of Monomeric and Oligomeric Metal Complexes|author=Weighardt, Karl|journal=Pure and Applied Chemistry|year=1988|volume=60|issue=4|pages=509–16|doi=10.1351/pac198860040509|s2cid=96871622|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 1994, he was appointed Director of the [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Energy Conversion|Max Planck Institute for Bioinorganic Chemistry]]. While at the Max Planck Institute, he developed a research program to study complexes of [[noninnocent ligand]]s.<ref name="Electronic_structure">{{cite journal 
 | title = Electronic Structure of Bis(imino)pyridine Iron Dichloride, Monochloride, and Neutral Ligand Complexes: A Combined Structural, Spectroscopic, and Computational Study
 |author1=Bart, S.C. |author2=Chlopek, K. |author3=Bill, E. |author4=Bouwkamp M.W. |author5=Lobkovsky, E. |author6=Nesse, F. |author7=Weighardt, K. |author8=Chirik, P. J. | journal = J. Am. Chem. Soc.
 | volume = 128
 | issue = 42
 | pages = 13901–13912
 | year = 2006
 | doi = 10.1021/ja064557b

</ref> Since 2010, he has been professor emeritus.<ref>{{cite web|title=MPI für chemische Energiekonversion: Prof. Dr. Karl Wieghardt: Vita|website=www.cec.mpg.de|url=https://www.cec.mpg.de/mitarbeiter/emeriti/prof-dr-karl-wieghardt/vita.html|access-date=2016-10-05}}</ref>

==Awards==
* [[Gay-Lussac Humboldt Prize|Gay-Lussac-Humboldt Prize]] (1995)
* [[Wilhelm Klemm]] Award from the [[Gesellschaft Deutscher Chemiker|German Chemical Society]] (2000)
*John C. Bailar Medal (2000)
* [[Centenary Prize]] of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (2001)
* Ruhr Prize for Arts and Sciences (2005)
* ACS Award in Inorganic Chemistry (2006)<ref>{{Cite web|title=ACS Award in Inorganic Chemistry|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-in-inorganic-chemistry.html|access-date=2021-05-17|website=American Chemical Society|language=en}}</ref>
* Elected member of the [[Academy of Sciences Leopoldina|German National Academy of Natural Sciences Leopoldina]] (2006)
